book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

chapters.file: ch04 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch06 - The Devils Get Their Due.md
chapters.relation: Editor Ben Dyer's introduction argues that supervillains have effectively 'won' as comics matured: since the 1970s-80s turn (O'Neil/Adams Green Lantern, Miller's Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen), heroes like Batman, Superman, and Spider-Man acquired broken psychologies while villains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Lex Luthor were humanized until hero and villain barely contrast. Citing Stan Lee's claim that the supervillain is the most important character, Dyer announces the volume's project: to restore that contrast by analyzing the villain's relation to morality and society, asking whether tyranny can serve a good cause, whether an all-powerful being is limitless, whether anyone can truly desire evil, and why good henchmen are so hard to find.

Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.

Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.

Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.

Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.

Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.

holes.name: Reflective Equilibrium
holes.what: A method (devised by Nelson Goodman, popularized by John Rawls) that starts from considered judgments and adjusts principles and judgments against each other until they cohere.
holes.why: Chapter 7's 'Making the A-List' openly builds its ranking of great supervillains on this method, framing it as a villain's way to 'cheat' at evaluation instead of deriving criteria first.

holes.name: Underdetermination of Theory by Data
holes.what: The thesis that empirical evidence never uniquely fixes a single theory, since incompatible alternatives can fit the same data equally well.
holes.why: Chapter 7's mad-science essay makes underdetermination the engine of its argument that theory choice necessarily smuggles in the scientist's values, and that denying this is precisely what makes science 'mad'.

holes.name: Intellectualism vs Voluntarism (will and intellect)
holes.what: The medieval debate over whether the will must choose what the intellect presents as best (Aquinas's intellectualism) or can choose against that judgment (Ockham's voluntarism).
holes.why: Chapter 8's Magneto essay is constructed entirely on this debate, concluding the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment and so supervillains always act for what seems good to them.

holes.name: Moral Nihilism / Error Theory
holes.what: The meta-ethical view, argued by J.L. Mackie via the 'argument from queerness', that there are no objective moral facts, so positive moral judgments are systematically in error.
holes.why: Chapter 8's meta-ethics essay gives nihilism equal billing with relativism and objectivism (testing it against Superman, the Red Skull, and moral disagreement), but the taxonomy has no slug for it.

holes.name: Moral Community (moral agents and patients)
holes.what: The circle of beings owed moral consideration, divided into moral agents who can act morally and moral patients who can be affected morally, gated by criteria such as rationality.
holes.why: Chapter 10's X-Men essay defines mutant superiority by asking who belongs to the moral community and on what characteristics, a framing concept the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Omnipotence (and its paradoxes)
holes.what: The property of being all-powerful, classically probed by puzzles such as the stone too heavy to lift and whether the logically impossible falls within divine power.
holes.why: Chapter 11's opening essay is wholly an analysis of what limits an all-powerful being, applied to the Beyonder, Doctor Doom, and Galactus, and no taxonomy slug covers omnipotence.
